learningObjectives.title: Brønsted–Lowry acids donate protons; bases accept them
Kw and the balance between H⁺ and OH⁻
Strong and weak, concentrated and dilute
Neutralization and the parents of a salt
The pH curve for a strong acid and strong base

questions.q: Copper(II) oxide, CuO, is insoluble in water. It reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form copper(II) sulfate and water. How should copper(II) oxide be classified?
options: As an alkali, as it neutralizes an acid
As a base, but it is not an alkali
As neither, as it contains no OH⁻ ions
As neither, since it is insoluble in water
optionWhy: Neutralizing an acid shows that CuO is a base, but 'alkali' means a base that is soluble in water and releases OH⁻(aq). Insoluble CuO is a base but not an alkali.
CuO accepts protons from the acid (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), so it is a base. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to release OH⁻(aq); CuO is insoluble, so it is not an alkali.
A Brønsted–Lowry base need not contain OH⁻; it must accept protons. The oxide ion in CuO accepts H⁺ to form water, so CuO is a base (though not an alkali).
Proton transfer does not require the base to dissolve in water first. CuO accepts protons from sulfuric acid, so it is a base; its insolubility is only why it is not an alkali.
questions.explain: CuO accepts protons from the acid (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), so it is a base. An alkali is a base that dissolves in water to release OH⁻(aq); CuO is insoluble, so it is not an alkali.

questions.q: What is the formula of the conjugate base of ethanoic acid, CH₃COOH?
options: CH₃COO
CH₃COO⁻
CH₃COOH₂⁺
CH₂COOH⁻
optionWhy: A proton is H⁺, not a hydrogen atom. Removing H⁺ from a neutral molecule leaves a species with a charge of −1: CH₃COO⁻, not the neutral CH₃COO.

The conjugate base is formed when the acid donates one proton, H⁺. Ethanoic acid loses the hydrogen of its –COOH group, so the formula loses one H and the charge falls by one: CH₃COOH → CH₃COO⁻ (the ethanoate ion).
CH₃COOH₂⁺ is formed when ethanoic acid GAINS a proton, so it is the conjugate acid of CH₃COOH. The conjugate base is the species left after the acid has donated its proton, CH₃COO⁻.
Only the hydrogen of the –COOH group is released as a proton; the C–H hydrogens of the methyl group are not acidic. Losing the O–H proton gives CH₃COO⁻.
questions.explain: The conjugate base is formed when the acid donates one proton, H⁺. Ethanoic acid loses the hydrogen of its –COOH group, so the formula loses one H and the charge falls by one: CH₃COOH → CH₃COO⁻ (the ethanoate ion).

questions.q: Which is a correct equation for HCO₃⁻ acting as a Brønsted–Lowry base in the forward reaction?
options: HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) ⇌ H₂CO₃⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
HCO₃⁻(aq) + OH⁻(aq) ⇌ CO₃²⁻(aq) + H₂O(l)
H₂CO₃(aq) + CH₃COO⁻(aq) ⇌ HCO₃⁻(aq) + CH₃COOH(aq)
HCO₃⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq) ⇌ H₂CO₃(aq) + H₂O(l)
optionWhy: Gaining H⁺ raises the charge by one unit, so HCO₃⁻ becomes H₂CO₃, not H₂CO₃⁻. As written, the charge does not balance: 0 on the left, −1 on the right.
Here HCO₃⁻ loses a proton to OH⁻, becoming CO₃²⁻: that is acid behaviour. A Brønsted–Lowry base accepts a proton, as HCO₃⁻ does with H₃O⁺.
In the forward reaction HCO₃⁻ is formed, when H₂CO₃ donates a proton to CH₃COO⁻; it is the conjugate base of H₂CO₃ but is not acting as a base. It accepts a proton only in the reverse reaction.
HCO₃⁻ gains a proton from H₃O⁺, becoming H₂CO₃: gaining H⁺ is what a Brønsted–Lowry base does. Its charge rises by one, from −1 to 0, and the equation balances in atoms and charge.
questions.explain: HCO₃⁻ gains a proton from H₃O⁺, becoming H₂CO₃: gaining H⁺ is what a Brønsted–Lowry base does. Its charge rises by one, from −1 to 0, and the equation balances in atoms and charge.

questions.q: 10.0 cm³ of hydrochloric acid of pH 1.70 is diluted with distilled water to a total volume of 1.00 dm³ at 298 K. What is [H⁺] in the diluted solution?
options: 0.00020 mol dm⁻³
0.020 mol dm⁻³
0.50 mol dm⁻³
0.0018 mol dm⁻³
optionWhy: [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ in the original acid. Amount of H⁺ = 0.0200 × 0.0100 dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol, in 1.00 dm³, so [H⁺] = 0.00020 mol dm⁻³ (a 100-fold dilution).
0.020 mol dm⁻³ is [H⁺] in the original acid, 10⁻¹·⁷⁰. Diluting 10.0 cm³ to 1.00 dm³ makes the solution 100 times less concentrated: [H⁺] = 0.00020 mol dm⁻³.
This uses 10¹·⁷⁰ = 50 mol dm⁻³ for the original acid, dropping the minus sign: [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ. A solution of pH above 0 has [H⁺] below 1 mol dm⁻³; here 0.020 mol dm⁻³, diluted to 0.00020 mol dm⁻³.
This uses e⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.18, the natural antilogarithm. pH is defined with log₁₀, so [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.020 mol dm⁻³, diluted 100-fold to 0.00020 mol dm⁻³.
questions.explain: [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ in the original acid. Amount of H⁺ = 0.0200 × 0.0100 dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol, in 1.00 dm³, so [H⁺] = 0.00020 mol dm⁻³ (a 100-fold dilution).
questions.working: [H⁺] in the original acid = 10⁻ᵖᴴ = 10⁻¹·⁷⁰ = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³. n(H⁺) = 0.0200 mol dm⁻³ × (10.0/1000) dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol. [H⁺] after dilution = 2.00 × 10⁻⁴ mol ÷ 1.00 dm³ = 0.00020 mol dm⁻³ (2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³).

questions.q: A student's data show that an aqueous solution at 323 K has [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 2.34 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³, so its pH is 6.63. Which statement about this solution is correct?
options: It is neutral, as its [H⁺] and [OH⁻] are equal.
It is acidic, as its pH is lower than 7.00.
It is acidic, as it contains H⁺(aq) ions.
Both acidic and basic: each ion exceeds 1.0 × 10⁻⁷.
optionWhy: A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻], at any temperature. pH 7.00 marks neutrality only at 298 K; at 323 K a neutral solution has a lower pH because water is more ionized.
pH 7.00 is the neutral point only at 298 K. The test is the relative size of [H⁺] and [OH⁻]; here they are equal, so the solution is neutral even though its pH is 6.63.
Every aqueous solution contains both H⁺ and OH⁻ ions. A solution is acidic only when [H⁺] > [OH⁻]; here they are equal, so it is neutral.

Acidic and basic are judged by comparing [H⁺] with [OH⁻], not by comparing each with its 298 K value. The two are equal here, so the solution is neutral; 1.0 × 10⁻⁷ mol dm⁻³ is the neutral value only at 298 K.
questions.explain: A solution is neutral when [H⁺] = [OH⁻], at any temperature. pH 7.00 marks neutrality only at 298 K; at 323 K a neutral solution has a lower pH because water is more ionized.

questions.q:
Hydrogen chloride reacts with water:
HCl(aq) + H₂O(l) → H₃O⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq)
The position of this equilibrium lies so far to the right that the reaction is effectively complete. Which statement about this reaction is correct?
options: Cl⁻ is the acid, since HCl forms it.
Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O.
H₃O⁺ is a stronger acid than HCl.
H₂O is the acid, as it gains a proton.
optionWhy: Cl⁻ is what remains after HCl donates its proton: it is the conjugate base of HCl, not an acid. The acid in the forward reaction is HCl, the reactant that loses H⁺.
Acid–base equilibria lie on the side of the weaker acid and weaker base. The products, H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻, are favoured, so Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O (and H₃O⁺ a weaker acid than HCl).
An equilibrium lies on the side of the weaker acid. H₃O⁺ is favoured, so it is the weaker acid; HCl, which gives up its proton almost completely, is the stronger.

Gaining a proton makes H₂O the Brønsted–Lowry base here; HCl donates the proton and is the acid. Because the equilibrium lies to the right, the products are the weaker acid and base, so Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O.
questions.explain: Acid–base equilibria lie on the side of the weaker acid and weaker base. The products, H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻, are favoured, so Cl⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O (and H₃O⁺ a weaker acid than HCl).

questions.q: Separate 25.0 cm³ samples of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH(aq) are each titrated with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq). Which statement is correct?
options: Both need the same volume of NaOH(aq), as the acid amounts are equal.
The HCl needs more NaOH(aq), as it releases more H⁺ ions in water.
Both acids start at the same pH, as their acid concentrations are equal.
The CH₃COOH starts at the lower pH, as each molecule has four H atoms.
optionWhy: Both samples contain 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of a monoprotic acid, so both need 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of NaOH (25.0 cm³). As OH⁻ removes H⁺, the ethanoic acid equilibrium shifts to the right until all the acid has reacted.
HCl does have the higher [H⁺] at the start, but the amount of base needed depends on the amount of acid. Ethanoic acid keeps ionizing as its H⁺ is removed, so both need 25.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq).
Only a strong acid has [H⁺] equal to its concentration. HCl is fully ionized (pH 1.0); ethanoic acid is only slightly ionized, so its [H⁺] is lower and its starting pH higher.
Only the H of the –COOH group in ethanoic acid can ionize, and only partly. CH₃COOH is a weak monoprotic acid, so its [H⁺] is lower than that of HCl and its pH is higher.
questions.explain: Both samples contain 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of a monoprotic acid, so both need 2.50 × 10⁻³ mol of NaOH (25.0 cm³). As OH⁻ removes H⁺, the ethanoic acid equilibrium shifts to the right until all the acid has reacted.

questions.q: At 298 K, 0.10 mol dm⁻³ aqueous solutions have these pH values: HCl 1.0; CH₃COOH 2.9; NH₃ 11.1; NaOH 13.0. Which conclusion is supported by these data?
options: HCl is only partly ionized in solution, as its pH is 1.0 rather than 0.0.
NH₃ is a strong base, as its solution has a pH well above 7, at 11.1.
NH₃(aq) needs less HCl(aq) than an equal volume of NaOH(aq) does.
CH₃COOH is a weak acid, as its [H⁺] is far below 0.10 mol dm⁻³.
optionWhy: pH 1.0 corresponds to [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, exactly the concentration of the acid, so every HCl molecule has ionized. pH 0.0 would need [H⁺] = 1.0 mol dm⁻³, ten times more than is present.

An alkaline pH shows only that OH⁻ is present. pH 11.1 gives [H⁺] = 7.9 × 10⁻¹² mol dm⁻³, so [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺] ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 1% of the 0.10 mol dm⁻³ ammonia; the strong base NaOH at the same concentration reaches pH 13.0. NH₃ is a weak base.

Equal volumes of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq) and NaOH(aq) contain equal amounts of base and need equal amounts of HCl. As the acid reacts, the NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ equilibrium shifts right until all the ammonia has reacted; these pH data say nothing about the titre.

pH 2.9 means [H⁺] = 10⁻²·⁹ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, only about 1% of the 0.10 mol dm⁻³ acid. Most of the CH₃COOH is un-ionized, which is what 'weak' means. HCl at the same concentration gives pH 1.0, [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³: complete ionization.
questions.explain: pH 2.9 means [H⁺] = 10⁻²·⁹ ≈ 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, only about 1% of the 0.10 mol dm⁻³ acid. Most of the CH₃COOH is un-ionized, which is what 'weak' means. HCl at the same concentration gives pH 1.0, [H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³: complete ionization.
questions.working: HCl: pH 1.0 gives [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·⁰ = 0.10 mol dm⁻³, equal to the acid concentration (complete ionization). CH₃COOH: pH 2.9 gives [H⁺] = 10⁻²·⁹ = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 1% of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (partial ionization). NaOH: pH 13.0 gives [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻¹³, so [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺] = 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (complete). NH₃: pH 11.1 gives [H⁺] = 7.9 × 10⁻¹², [OH⁻] = 1.3 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³, about 1% of 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (partial).

questions.q: Solid magnesium oxide, MgO, is added to dilute nitric acid, HNO₃(aq). Which statement about what happens is correct?
options: MgO and HNO₃ react in a 1 : 1 mole ratio, as NaOH and HCl do too.
No reaction occurs, as MgO is not a base: it has no hydroxide ions.
Hydrogen gas is released, as acids give off H₂ in their reactions.
MgO and HNO₃ react in a 1 : 2 mole ratio, as O²⁻ accepts two H⁺.
optionWhy: NaOH and HCl react 1 : 1 because OH⁻ accepts one proton. O²⁻ accepts two (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), and Mg²⁺ needs two NO₃⁻: MgO + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂O, so the ratio is 1 : 2.
A Brønsted–Lowry base need not contain OH⁻. The oxide ion accepts protons, forming water, so MgO is a base and neutralizes nitric acid: MgO + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂O.
Hydrogen forms when an acid reacts with a reactive metal. With a metal oxide the protons are accepted by O²⁻, forming water: MgO + 2HNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + H₂O. No gas is produced.
MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l). The oxide ion accepts two H⁺ (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), and the salt Mg(NO₃)₂ needs two NO₃⁻ for each Mg²⁺, so 1 mol of MgO reacts with 2 mol of HNO₃.
questions.explain: MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l). The oxide ion accepts two H⁺ (O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O), and the salt Mg(NO₃)₂ needs two NO₃⁻ for each Mg²⁺, so 1 mol of MgO reacts with 2 mol of HNO₃.
questions.working: MgO(s) + 2HNO₃(aq) → Mg(NO₃)₂(aq) + H₂O(l). Atoms: Mg 1 = 1; N 2 = 2; O 1 + 6 = 6 + 1; H 2 = 2. O²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O, so n(HNO₃) : n(MgO) = 2 : 1.

questions.q: Solid sodium hydrogencarbonate, NaHCO₃, is added to dilute hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq). Which statement about the reaction is correct?
options: NaHCO₃ and HCl react in a 1 : 1 mole ratio, as HCO₃⁻ accepts one H⁺.
NaHCO₃ and HCl react in a 1 : 2 mole ratio, as carbonates do.
Only NaCl and water form, as neutralization gives salt and water.
Hydrogen gas is released, as acids give H₂ when they react.
optionWhy: NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). HCO₃⁻ accepts one H⁺ and the product breaks down to water and carbon dioxide, which is released as a gas: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
The 1 : 2 ratio belongs to the carbonate ion, which accepts two protons (CO₃²⁻ + 2H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂). HCO₃⁻ already carries one H, so it accepts only one: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
'Acid + base → salt + water' is incomplete for hydrogencarbonates. HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, so carbon dioxide is also produced and the mixture fizzes.
Hydrogen forms when an acid reacts with a reactive metal. Here the proton is accepted by HCO₃⁻, and the gas released is carbon dioxide: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.
questions.explain: NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). HCO₃⁻ accepts one H⁺ and the product breaks down to water and carbon dioxide, which is released as a gas: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂.
questions.working: NaHCO₃(s) + HCl(aq) → NaCl(aq) + H₂O(l) + CO₂(g). Atoms: Na 1 = 1; H 1 + 1 = 2; C 1 = 1; O 3 = 1 + 2; Cl 1 = 1. HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂, so n(HCl) : n(NaHCO₃) = 1 : 1.

questions.q: 25.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) is placed in a flask and 0.100 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq) is added from a burette. The figure shows four sketched pH curves, A to D. Which curve shows how the pH in the flask changes?
options: Curve C
Curve B
Curve A
Curve D
optionWhy: The flask starts with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq), pH 13. Added acid is neutralized while the pH stays high, then at 25.0 cm³ (n(HCl) = n(NaOH)) the pH falls almost vertically through 7, and excess HCl(aq) takes the pH down towards 1.5. Only panel C has this shape.

The intercept on the pH axis is the pH of the solution in the FLASK before any titrant is added, not that of the HCl(aq) in the burette. The flask holds NaOH(aq), so the curve must start near pH 13 and fall, as in panel C.

pH is logarithmic, so it does not change in proportion to the volume added. While NaOH is in excess the pH changes little; near 25.0 cm³ one drop changes it by several units, giving the steep section of panel C, not a straight line.
After equivalence the added HCl(aq) is in excess and the solution becomes acidic, so the pH keeps falling below 7 and levels off near 1.5, as in panel C. It does not stay at 7.
questions.explain: The flask starts with 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq), pH 13. Added acid is neutralized while the pH stays high, then at 25.0 cm³ (n(HCl) = n(NaOH)) the pH falls almost vertically through 7, and excess HCl(aq) takes the pH down towards 1.5. Only panel C has this shape.

figure.alt: Four small pH curves, pH 0 to 14 (ticks 0, 7, 14 and a dashed line at pH 7) against volume of HCl(aq) added / cm³ (no scale shown). Panel A: a straight line falling steadily from pH 13 to about pH 1. Panel B: starts near pH 1, stays low, rises almost vertically about halfway along the axis through pH 7 and levels off near pH 12.5. Panel C: starts near pH 13, stays high, falls almost vertically about halfway along the axis through pH 7 and levels off near pH 1.5. Panel D: starts near pH 13, falls almost vertically about halfway along the axis to pH 7 and then stays horizontal at pH 7.

questions.q: The graph shows the pH curve obtained when 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH(aq) is added to 25.0 cm³ of HCl(aq). What is the concentration of the HCl(aq)?
options: 1.25 × 10⁻¹ mol dm⁻³
8.00 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³
1.00 × 10⁻¹ mol dm⁻³
4.44 × 10⁻² mol dm⁻³
optionWhy: This inverts the volume ratio (25.0/20.0). The acid needed the LARGER volume of the two solutions, so it is the less concentrated: 25.0 cm³ of acid contains the same amount as 20.0 cm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ NaOH, so c(HCl) = 0.100 × 20.0/25.0 = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³.

Equivalence is at the middle of the steep section, 20.0 cm³. n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol = n(HCl), so c(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³. The intercept at pH 1.1 confirms it: 10⁻¹·¹ ≈ 0.08 mol dm⁻³.
Equivalence means equal AMOUNTS (mol), not equal concentrations or volumes. 20.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq), not 25.0 cm³, neutralizes the acid, so the acid is less concentrated than the base: 0.0800 mol dm⁻³.
This divides 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol by the total volume at equivalence, 45.0 cm³. The acid was all in the 25.0 cm³ placed in the flask, so c(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³.
questions.explain: Equivalence is at the middle of the steep section, 20.0 cm³. n(NaOH) = 0.100 × 0.0200 = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol = n(HCl), so c(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ / 0.0250 = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³. The intercept at pH 1.1 confirms it: 10⁻¹·¹ ≈ 0.08 mol dm⁻³.
questions.working: The equivalence point is at the middle of the near-vertical section, at 20.0 cm³ of NaOH(aq). n(NaOH) = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.0200 dm³ = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol. HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O, so n(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol. c(HCl) = 2.00 × 10⁻³ mol / 0.0250 dm³ = 0.0800 mol dm⁻³. Check: the intercept, pH 1.1, gives [H⁺] = 10⁻¹·¹ = 0.08 mol dm⁻³, consistent with a fully ionized 0.0800 mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq).
